content: After a few verbs and adjectives of
demand, English keeps a BARE verb — no
-s, no does, no past.
"We recommend that he be told at once."
not "that he is told."
"They insisted that she stay."
"It is essential that the door remain
shut."
The trigger words are few:
recommend, insist, demand, propose,
suggest, request — and
vital, essential, important, crucial.
The bare form does not change for he,
she or it, and its negative takes no do:
"We ask that he not be disturbed."
British English often prefers should:
"We recommend that he should be told."
Both are correct; the bare form is
crisper and more formal.
Many languages have a full subjunctive
for this. English has only this one
surviving corner of its own.
When the source does not matter, or you
will not name it, English reports at a
distance.
it + be + said/believed/reported + that:
"It is said that the leak came from
inside."
"It was believed that nobody survived."
"It is reported that talks have failed."
The same idea can hang on the subject
instead:
subject + be + thought + to + verb.
"He is thought to be abroad."
"She is believed to have left already."
Watch the two times: to be = now,
to have left = before the report.
This is the register of news, science
and officialdom. It states a thing
without promising who said it.
Many languages use an impersonal 'one
says' or a reporting mood; English uses
the passive and an empty it.
Careful English grades a claim instead
of shouting it.
seem / appear to = it looks that way.
"The figures appear to be wrong."
tend to = usually, not always.
"Prices tend to rise in spring."
be likely to = probably.
"He is likely to refuse."
Single words do the same work:
apparently = so people say.
presumably = I assume so.
arguably = a case can be made.
"Arguably the best result of the year."
And to flip a claim outright:
on the contrary = the opposite is true.
"It did not help. On the contrary, it
made things worse."
Careful: on the contrary CONTRADICTS;
in contrast merely compares.
Many languages hedge with a particle or
a verb ending; English spends whole
words on it — and expects them.
